body_markdown:
Not all makeshift repairs are created equal, but odds are that any one of them will make a fantastic story. That was my hope when asking Hagerty Media readers to share their worst (best?) repair performed when the chips were down. Once again, they didn’t let me down. I’ve selected a representative handful for this piece, but I could have added many more, so I suggest you take a look at the original thread[here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/hagerty-community/whats-your-worst-makeshift-repair/) , to see even more of the best worst makeshift repairs.


I am confident that you will enjoy this selection, as you folks are amazing storytellers! And if you didn’t comment the first time around, we’d love to hear about your own makeshift repair in the comments section.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


**Don J:** In the early ’90s, three buddies in a borrowed VW Rabbit overheated deep in the Baja. We dried the distributor system and needed to add coolant to the radiator but we had no coolant. What to do? We did, however, have full bladders from drinking lots of beer and water.


You gotta do what ya gotta do. We made it into town!


Flickr/Don Barrett


**Edward A:** In 1971 I went to Death Valley in a Renault Dauphine and made a 30-mile side trip on a dirt road to the dry lake “racetrack” where boulders leave mysterious tracks in the playa. About halfway back, a front tire kicked up a rock that ripped out the fuel tank drain plug, and I lost all my gasoline.


Fortunately, I had a gallon of Coleman fuel for my camp stove, so I put it in the engine compartment and used the vacuum advance hose to go from the Coleman can to the fuel pump inlet, and then drove slowly on ~50 octane gas to Scotty’s Castle, which had the nearest filling station but no garage service.


The engine was “dieseling” at the end of that drive and couldn’t be turned off with the ignition key, so I had to hand choke the engine off by putting my palm over the air intake. It was then near closing time, so I made a quick survey in their gift shop for something to plug my fuel tank and found a small wiggly rubber monster.


I pulled its arms and legs off and stuffed it into the hole in the bottom of the fuel tank and was able to fill up the Dauphine with 7 (!) gallons of real gasoline and then drive normally back to Southern California. About a week later, the gasoline shrank and hardened the rubber monster enough so that it was leaking, so I found a rubber plug that was gasoline-resistant and ran the car with that for several more years. I later found out that a bar of soap can be cut down to use as a gas-tank plug in an emergency.


1969 Chevy Van


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


**Craig:** The engine of my first car, a 1970 Chevy van, was located between the seats in its doghouse. The neutral switch either broke, wore out, or became dislodged—50 years later, I’m still not sure. My starting ritual was: Flip the two latches holding the engine cover down, grab the screwdriver from “its location” in the dash, lean over from the driver’s seat to the passenger side of the engine, and arc the posts on the solenoid to engage the starter.


I did that for three or four years, until I sold the van. Looking back, I probably should have amended my ritual by adding “make sure the automatic transmission was in park or neutral” before arcing…fun times!


Dodge


**Binksman:** A year and a half ago I replaced an O-ring on the inlet pipe to the water pump on my Dodge Magnum. The bolt that holds the metal pipe snapped flush in the aluminum timing cover. In my haste, I ZipTied the pipe to a bolt, then added another ZipTie around the first and the head of another bolt to maintain its tension.


Long story short, the fix worked well enough that I forgot about it until recently. Now the water pump is going out, and I happened to notice that the replaced O-ring is leaking again because the ZipTies (after many heat cycles) are starting to loosen. I have all the parts to repair everything properly, just no time to do so!


YouTube/Volvo Cars


**Colton:** When the wiper motor died in a college friend’s Volvo 240, we pulled the glove box and the front passenger would run the wipers by hand, as the linkage was accessible with the glove box removed.


We did a cross-border run to grab the replacement wiper motor on a break between classes. The wiper motor bolts in from under the hood, and the linkage gets re-assembled in the car. So we bolted the motor in, then I spent the 30-minute drive back to school with my arms buried in the dash, re-assembling the wiper linkage by hand. I had to hurry, as it started to rain halfway.


That is the only time I’ve re-assembled part of a car while en route.


Mecum


**Ben:** In my younger years, I was raking hay in a field far from our farm using our 1947 Ford 8N tractor. At some point, the bolt that holds the generator bracket vibrated loose and dropped somewhere in the field. This caused the generator (and the needle on the ammeter gauge) to flop around. Concerned that the fan belt would come out of its pulleys and break, I shut off the engine and tried to find something to wedge against the generator to tighten the belt so I could get back to the farm to repair it.


Finding no other alternative, I took off one of my shoes and wedged it between the engine block and generator. It worked, and I made it back to the farm.


ICON


**John T:** In 1977, towing a Corvette race car with a ’72 Suburban, in the middle of the night (of course), the upper radiator hose on the Suburban blew. I took the upper hose off the Corvette, cut the aluminum filler neck off the thermostat housing, joined a couple pieces of radiator hoses together to get us back home. The rest of the trip from Hutchinson, Kansas, to Omaha, Nebraska, was uneventful.


Jordan Lewis


**Gerard P:** I once fixed a friend’s Jeep Cherokee broken driveshafts by pulling the front out and holding the back one in place with my belt to get home. I will *never* do a four-wheel-drive holeshot again!


Flickr/BiERLOS


**James G:** While traveling through Montreal in my ’68 Dodge Coronet, I hit the world’s deepest pothole and blew out an air shock. I could not find a replacement within a two-day drive, so I crawled underneath, pulled the air boot back over the top half of the shock, secured it with two gear clamps, refilled the system with a can of tire sealant and some air and motored on. I met up with the kit deep into Nova Scotia, convinced a one-man shop to remove the old and install the new, and carried on with our vacation. Did I mention that I was pulling a hardtop pop-up trailer?


The tech loved the temp repair so much that he hung it on his wall of shame!


## Swing for the Fences


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


**Brad N:** About 50 years ago (yes, I’m that old), I was traveling home to LA on Interstate 5 when my ’66 Chevy pickup gave up the rear muffler support bracket. I just needed some safety or bailing wire to rehang the exhaust, but I had nothing on board, only a pair of pliers. The nearby chain-link fence had some barbed wire at the top, so I cut off a couple of feet and managed to secure the muffler well enough to drive home. Working with barbed wire is not ideal (!) but the stuff is strong, and the repair lasted until I could fix the bracket properly a couple of weeks later.


**Herbert W:** Last year I was helping move my granddaughter and her husband to Texas. We were in West Texas, in the middle of nowhere, on I-10. My Ford 350 crew cab with a 7.3 was loaded to almost 113,000 pounds with the loaded car on a tow dolly. The power steering pressure hose blew out of the housing. It was a lousy design for a pressure hose; I could push it back in, but the seal was gone.


There was a fence just off the road with an added wire to hold the fence down. There was extra wire that I was able to cut off, and I wound it around the hose just behind the metal portion and then pulled it tight around the filler neck. It held until I stopped at a gas station to see where I could find someplace to get parts. As I turned in, the hose blew out again.


One of the patrons there said there was a parts house about 10 miles down the highway. I got in and drove on down the highway, afraid that with no oil in it the pump would be destroyed. I found the parts house and bought a new hose, put it in, and refilled the system, and everything worked good and has since. Sometimes it is better to be lucky than good…


## Cables and Cords


A custom-turned knob and bracket to hold a bungee cord.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


**rogerd:** This will be a two-part answer. Part one happened while riding an early ’70s CB750 to work one day. About an hour ride from New Hampshire to Ipswich, Massachusetts, one of the two throttle cables snapped—the one to advance throttle, of course. I finished the second half of the ride by disconnecting the cable from the handgrip and pulling the cable straight out to the right side to accelerate. Fun times.


Now for part two. With a complete lack of parts and just the basic bike toolkit, the only option I had was to connect the throttle return cable to the advance side of the carb rack. There was no way to connect the cable to the advance side of the handgrip, though, so the throttle was backward for the ride home.


It was an improvement—both hands on the bars again, but…. still a rough ride.


**drjim:** The throttle cable snapped on my ’75 VW Dasher GT. Since I do field service work, I had a lot of tools and “stuff” in the back. I wound up snaking a length of 16AWG wire through the jacket, cable-tying it to the throttle lever on the carb, and putting a big loop to hold onto so I could open and close the throttle by hand. It was a chore to work the throttle with my right hand and use the clutch and gearshift at the same time.


It was OK on the highway because I could tie the wire to the console, and I had a basic cruise control.


**Timothy V:** When the carburetor linkage clip broke, I used a bungee cord as a repair. It got me home.


**Jeff F:** I had an old 1970s 19-foot Sea Ray boat with a Chevy six-cylinder (dubbed a Rambler engine at the time in the late ’70s) that developed a broken fan belt when I was fishing off the coast of San Diego. Of course, there was no spare, and my friend grabbed the broken belt and tossed it overboard out of frustration. I makeshifted a belt out of a piece of anchor line and fishing line to thread the rope together. It actually worked. We made it back to the boat ramp at Shelter Island. From Ocean Beach into San Diego Bay.


**Dave:** I once had to use jumper cables as a throttle return. It was late, and the gas pedal would stick and not return. I clamped the jaws of the jumper cables to the metal rod of the gas pedal inside the car and would pull the cables to close the throttle. The next day I found out that the line for the oil pressure gauge was hooked around the linkage under the dashboard.


## A Shaft of Light


Flickr/Peter Marheine


**Scott R:** One day in the fall of 1976 I had put new bolts in my license plate holders in my 1963 MGB. A few days later I had to go pick up a friend from the bus station in Washington, D.C., a 1.5-hour trip from where I lived. It was late at night and raining. After I picked him up and drove away from the bus station, I heard a weird noise and felt a thumping in the transmission tunnel of the car. I got out and looked under the car and saw my driveshaft hanging.


It was late and raining, but fortunately I had left the wrenches in my car. I was much thinner then and was able to crawl under the MG, which is pretty close to the ground. Being a freshman in college, I knew I didn’t have the money to call a tow truck to tow me 1.5 hours home! But then it hit me: The bolts in the license plate holders were long enough to fix the drive shaft! So I took two bolts from the front and two from the back plates and put them in the driveshaft. We made it home safely. In fact, they worked for two weeks before I could find the correct bolts!


**George P:** Driving a ’61 Econoline through Alabama headed for Panama City. The front universal went, and the driveshaft wound up under the left rear wheel. I checked it out briefly and hitched back to a small town through which we had just passed. A small auto parts store was still open, so I bought a new U-joint and headed back.


My friend Bill had crawled under to check things out and found that the front yoke of the transmission out shaft was cracked. While we were pondering this, the owner of the parts store pulled up behind. He wound up taking me around to at least three junkyards in the area. None of them had the yoke, so he dropped me off at the van with my thanks.


I wound up hammering the broken yoke back into some semblance of normal and putting in the new U-joint. It took us to Panama City and back to Atlanta, where my local junkyard promptly provided a new yoke.


## I’m Dizzy


Flickr/vtengr4047


**Bob W:** My Ford F-150 broke down around two in the morning somewhere between Kingman, Arizona, and Needles, California. I took a short nap waiting for a highway patrol to stop by and offer assistance. It became obvious that wasn’t going to happen, so I raised the hood as 18-wheelers roared past and pulled off the distributor cap and saw the router wasn’t moving when I shorted across the starter relay with a wrench.


I removed the distributor and saw a pin on the shaft had sheared, so I looked around in the pickup bed and found a nail about the right size, inserted it and pounded the ends over, put it back in and timed it by ear, and got back on the road. I think it was still there when I sold the truck a few years later.


**Mark G:** On the last day of the Carrera Panamericana, we were running about 145 mph and lost all power. Downshifted after it dropped speed, no help. Coasted out of the way and found that the rotor had loosened from the distributor. It was held by two little screws which we found in the dizzy. The cap was smashed into three pieces. We replaced the rotor and taped the cap together with bandage tape from the first aid kit. Missed that stage, but made it into Laredo.


## A Can-Do Attitude?


Rob Siegel


**Craig L:** I know this is a bit of a cheat, as I’m not talking about my own repair, but rather about a makeshift repair on a car we bought. I purchased a used 2012 Jeep Wrangler JK for my son about eight years ago. When I bought it, I noted that it had a basic aftermarket air intake. No problem, we could easily replace/upgrade that. However, when we did finally manage to pull it out, I noted that the cold air intake was made from a basic K&N filter, some tubing, pipe clamps, and two Campbell soup cans. Soup cans? What happened to the stock breather that made someone think that soup cans were an upgrade?


**Eric K:** Campbell soup cans are versatile. During an extremely low budget time in my life, the exhaust pipe on my 1965 Volvo 1800S broke in half. I used a can opener to remove both ends of a Campbell Soup can, slit it lengthwise, slipped it over the broken pipe, and clamped it in place with two hose clamps. I did remove the paper label so the paper wouldn’t catch fire. If I remember right, it lasted four or five months.


**MPH302:** My dad used a Quaker State one-quart oil can. Because the diameter of the can was greater than the diameter of the pipe, he was able to overlap the can on itself. That, two clamps, and some muffler putty made for a surprisingly quiet and durable repair.


**Niles:** I also did the can and muffler-putty fix. Not my finest moment, but as a college kid with a broken exhaust and no money to fix it, it was the best option.


**Eric:** I used a Jolt cola can to fabricate a breather for a Lotus Europa on vacation in Texas, and it was longer in service than I care to admit once we got back to Missouri. Ah, youth and spring break!
